tldr: The paper proposes FRDV, a motion retargeting pipeline that converts human motion capture data for humanoid robots at up to 9,156 frames per second (up to 136x faster than existing methods) using a custom SQP and Real-Time Iteration (RTI), while validating and refining physical plausibility via contact-implicit iLQR.
hero_caption: Motion retargeting of human movements to 12 different humanoid robots with vastly different body shapes and degrees of freedom using the proposed FRDV framework. By simply specifying keypoints on the hands, feet, and other sites, motions can be adapted instantly to diverse robot morphologies without retuning parameters.
overview:
When teaching diverse whole-body motions to humanoid robots, large-scale human motion capture (MoCap) datasets serve as an extremely appealing source of demonstrations. However, humans and robots differ in skeletal proportions, joint limits, and degrees of freedom. Motion retargeting—converting human movements into robot joint trajectories—is therefore essential. Historically, this conversion faced two major bottlenecks. First is the high computational cost: existing pipelines require over 40 hours to process large-scale datasets like AMASS (approx. 40 hours of real-time data across more than 10,000 clips), creating a bottleneck in rapid training loops. Second is retargeting quality: relying solely on geometric inverse kinematics (IK) often leads to ground penetration, floating feet, self-collisions, and foot skating, which cause downstream reinforcement learning (RL) tracking policies to fail.

To overcome these issues, the authors developed FRDV (Fast Retargeting with Dynamics Validation), a two-stage framework integrating rapid geometric conversion and physics-based validation. In the first stage, kinematic retargeting combines a custom Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) solver, Real-Time Iteration (RTI) that finishes in a single step per frame, and chunk-based temporal parallel processing, achieving a remarkable processing speed of up to 9,156 frames per second. In the second stage, an optimal control approach via Contact-Implicit iLQR verifies that torque limits and contact dynamics are satisfied, refining artifacts like foot sliding.

In evaluation experiments on the Unitree G1 robot using AMASS and LAFAN1 datasets, FRDV achieved a 136x to 191x speedup over existing pipelines (GMR and ProtoMotions). Training motion tracking policies with reinforcement learning (BeyondMimic) on the retargeted references demonstrated tracking fidelity and task success rates on par with or exceeding prior methods. Furthermore, the trajectory refinement via contact-implicit iLQR dramatically eliminated foot skating, and policies trained on the references were successfully transferred zero-shot to a real Unitree G1 humanoid, reproducing stable motions in reality.
contributions: Building an ultra-fast kinematic retargeting pipeline running at up to 9,156 FPS that avoids self-collision and ground penetration by integrating a custom SQP solver, Gauss-Newton approximation, Real-Time Iteration (RTI), and chunk-based parallel processing
Introducing a dynamic validation stage using Contact-Implicit iLQR under MuJoCo dynamics and torque limits to verify and refine motions, eliminating foot floating and foot skating

Extensively evaluating geometric adaptability across 12 diverse humanoid robot models, as well as tracking performance and success rates of downstream reinforcement learning (RL) policies trained on the generated trajectories
Demonstrating zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of motion tracking policies trained on FRDV-generated references directly onto a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot with stable motion reproduction

sections.heading: Why We Need Retargeting to Be Incredibly Fast Right Now
sections.summary: While training humanoid robots from large-scale human MoCap datasets is gaining traction, retargeting across morphological gaps has suffered from immense computation times and degraded quality. This paper proposes FRDV, a new framework combining ultra-fast kinematic retargeting at up to 9,156 FPS with contact-implicit dynamics validation (CI-iLQR).
sections.details:
In recent years, reinforcement learning (RL) utilizing large-scale human motion capture (MoCap) datasets such as AMASS and LAFAN1 has become popular for teaching humanoid robots whole-body locomotion and manipulation skills. However, human and robot skeletons differ completely in link lengths, joint ranges, and mass distributions. Motion retargeting—converting human keypoint trajectories into robot joint angles—is thus an indispensable preprocessing step.

Yet, existing pipelines have suffered from two major roadblocks:
- **Computational Efficiency Limits**: Existing pipelines like ProtoMotions require nearly two full days of compute to process the AMASS dataset (around 11,000 clips, over 40 hours of real-time motion). When scaling up to massive training datasets exceeding 100 million frames (around 700 hours), low processing throughput fatally bottlenecks experimental iteration cycles.
- **Retargeting Quality Issues**: Conversions that overlook morphological differences and joint limits frequently cause robot link self-collisions, ground penetration, and unnatural foot skating. These artifacts directly lead to downstream RL tracking policies falling over or failing.

The paper proposes FRDV (Fast Retargeting with Dynamics Validation) to tackle both challenges at once. Combining a custom SQP solver, Real-Time Iteration (RTI) from nonlinear MPC, and parallel processing across temporal chunks, it attains a speed of up to 9,156 FPS—a 136x to 191x speedup over existing methods like ProtoMotions and GMR. Furthermore, for physically questionable motions, it employs a two-stage design where Contact-Implicit iLQR (CI-iLQR) optimizes the trajectory under MuJoCo rigid-body contact dynamics and actuator torque limits, resolving foot sliding and floating.

sections.heading: Where Geometric IK Meets Contact Dynamics Optimization
sections.summary: Existing kinematic retargeting methods run at only tens of FPS due to the overhead of general-purpose solvers. This work achieves ultra-fast speeds by tailoring nonlinear MPC techniques (Gauss-Newton approximations and RTI) to retargeting, and uniquely pairs them with optimal control (CI-iLQR) that does not require pre-specifying contact sequences.
sections.details:
### II-A Challenges in Kinematic Retargeting
Approaches for mapping human poses to robots include frame-by-frame methods like GMR and OmniRetarget, whole-clip optimization like PHC, and ProtoMotions which considers neighboring frames. However, all of these operate at only a few tens of frames per second. Because recent foundation model approaches generate robot motion data exceeding 100 million frames, low throughput directly drives up data generation costs.

### II-B Formulation of Numerical Inverse Kinematics (IK)
Constrained nonlinear inverse kinematics has commonly relied on general-purpose nonlinear programming (NLP) solvers such as IPOPT or SNOPT. Due to their high generality, they incur large computational overhead, making them ill-suited for high-speed per-frame processing. GMR employs differential IK via Mink (solving a QP at each step), while ProtoMotions relies on PyRoki (Levenberg-Marquardt and augmented Lagrangian methods), but both still face speed challenges.
In contrast, this work builds a specialized SQP solver with a Gauss-Newton Hessian approximation. Because the objective function is a weighted sum of squared residuals, the Hessian is always positive semi-definite (convex). This allows the fast OSQP solver to run reliably. Furthermore, by exploiting temporal continuity to perform only a single SQP iteration per frame via Real-Time Iteration (RTI), the framework achieves exceptional lightweight computation.

### II-C Dynamics Validation and Contact-Implicit Optimal Control
Trajectories converted purely through kinematics may look geometrically sound, yet harbor physical contradictions such as exceeding robot torque limits or walking with feet floating in mid-air. Recent studies have explored sampling-based correction methods (like SPIDER and DynaRetarget), but their computational weight remains an issue. This paper adopts contact-implicit optimal control, which uses gradients to discover contact transitions without explicit contact scheduling, building a torque-constrained iLQR upon MuJoCo MPC to track and refine reference motions under full dynamics.

sections.heading: Inside FRDV: Ultra-Fast SQP and Physics-Consistent CI-iLQR
sections.summary: The first phase solves a constrained optimization problem incorporating capsule-based self-collision and ground penetration avoidance at extreme speeds using Gauss-Newton SQP, RTI, and chunk parallelization. The second phase uses the kinematic trajectory as a reference and runs a CI-iLQR controller satisfying MuJoCo rigid-body contact dynamics and torque limits to produce physically realizable trajectories.
sections.details:
### III-A IK Formulation and Constraints
The robot's whole-body configuration is denoted as $\mathbf{q} = [\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{root}}^T, \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{root}}^T, \mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{joints}}^T]^T$. Human MoCap keypoints are pre-scaled to the robot's morphology, defining target positions $\{\mathbf{p}^\star_{s,t}\}$ at each frame $t$.

The objective function $J(\mathbf{q})$ consists of three terms:
- **Tracking Term ($J_{\mathrm{track}}$)**: Squared Euclidean distance between forward kinematics site positions on the robot (hands, feet, pelvis, etc.) and MoCap target positions.
- **Regularization Term ($J_{\mathrm{reg}}$)**: Penalizes deviations from a nominal posture $\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{joints}}^{\mathrm{nom}}$ to resolve redundancy and preserve a natural stance.
- **Smoothing Term ($J_{\mathrm{smooth}}$)**: Penalizes displacements from the previous frame's solution to prevent frame-to-frame jitter (with quaternion differences evaluated via geodesic distance on $\mathrm{SO}(3)$).

Constraints include joint position and velocity limits, as well as strict inequality constraints: links are approximated by capsules to stay above the ground (preventing floor penetration), and a minimum clearance distance $\delta$ is enforced between capsule centerlines (preventing self-collision).

### III-B Ultra-Fast Computation via Gauss-Newton SQP and RTI
This nonlinear problem is solved via Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP). Computing the exact Hessian requires expensive second-order kinematics derivatives and risks non-convexity. Capitalizing on the sum-of-squares objective, the Gauss-Newton approximation $\mathbf{H}_k \approx \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{res}}^T \mathbf{W} \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{res}}$ yields a convex QP solved efficiently by OSQP. To guarantee global convergence, backtracking line search using an $L_1$ merit function (under Armijo conditions) is applied. Leveraging inter-frame continuity, after the initial few frames the solver switches to Real-Time Iteration (RTI) mode with just one iteration per frame, dramatically reducing computation per step.

### III-C Chunk-Based Parallel Processing and Boundary Refinement
Long motion sequences are split temporally into multiple chunks and retargeted in parallel across multiple worker processes. In each chunk, the initial frame is solved with several SQP iterations until convergence, followed by RTI for subsequent frames. However, because chunks are solved independently, differing local minima can create discontinuities at chunk boundaries. To remedy this, the RefineBoundary routine flags boundaries where velocity or acceleration norms exceed two standard deviations above the mean, re-optimizing the adjacent chunk warm-started from the preceding solution.

### III-D Contact-Implicit iLQR (Dynamic Validation and Refinement)
Kinematics alone cannot detect floating, sliding, or excessive torque demands. Hence, a finite-horizon optimal control problem (CI-iLQR) incorporating MuJoCo rigid-body contact dynamics is applied. By tracking kinematic trajectories under actuator torque limits, contact forces emerge naturally in MuJoCo's simulation. Infeasible trajectories are filtered out, while viable ones are refined so that foot sliding is corrected into physically consistent contact states.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: 136x Faster Processing, RL Tracking, and Real Unitree G1 Deployment
sections.summary: Evaluated on LAFAN1 and AMASS datasets, FRDV achieved up to 9,156 FPS (677 FPS with a single worker), processing the entire AMASS dataset in roughly one hour. Furthermore, reinforcement learning (BeyondMimic) tracking accuracy was verified, CI-iLQR effectively eliminated foot skating, and zero-shot deployment was successfully demonstrated on a physical Unitree G1.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Processing Speed Benchmarks and Morphological Versatility
Benchmarks were conducted on an AMD Ryzen Threadripper 9960X CPU using the LAFAN1 dataset on the Unitree G1 model.
- **Throughput**: With 20 parallel workers, FRDV achieved an average of 9,156 FPS without boundary refinement, and 1,947 FPS with refinement. Even a single worker ran at 677 FPS—roughly 10x faster than GPU-based ProtoMotions (~67 FPS) and 14x faster than GMR (~48 FPS). In a 20-worker setup, it reached approximately 136x the speed of ProtoMotions.
- **AMASS Dataset Processing**: On the massive 13,662-clip AMASS dataset, which takes over 40 hours with ProtoMotions, FRDV (20 workers) finished in only about 1 hour.
- **Solver Breakdown**: Enabling self-collision constraints roughly doubles QP preparation time due to capsule distance Jacobian calculations, but the OSQP solving time itself remains stable.
- **Morphological Versatility**: Across 12 humanoids with distinct torso and leg proportions (Unitree G1/H1, Berkeley Humanoid, Booster T1/K1, Fourier N1, Openloong, Pal Talos, etc.), motions adapted successfully simply by selecting tracking sites without any parameter retuning.

### IV-C Tracking Performance in Downstream Reinforcement Learning
To evaluate reference trajectory quality, BeyondMimic was used to train tracking policies for the Unitree G1 over 500 million environment steps.
Metrics included task success rate alongside global mean per-body-part position error ($E_{\mathrm{g-mpbpe}}$), anchor-relative error ($E_{\mathrm{a-mpbpe}}$), and orientation error ($E_{\mathrm{mpboe}}$). Policies trained on FRDV references achieved success rates on par with or higher than GMR and ProtoMotions, and achieved lower tracking errors across many categories. This demonstrates that ultra-fast geometric retargeting does not sacrifice downstream learning quality.

### IV-D Impact of CI-iLQR Dynamic Validation
When applied to an aggressive one-leg hopping motion (LAFAN1) on G1 and Dash robots, CI-iLQR produced stable grounded trajectories within torque limits. Moreover, foot skating and foot floating—unavoidable in purely kinematic retargeting—were refined by CI-iLQR to establish firm, non-slip ground contact governed by MuJoCo's contact model.

### IV-E Sim-to-Real Transfer on the Physical Unitree G1
RL policies trained to track FRDV references were deployed zero-shot onto the real Unitree G1 humanoid. Without hardware-specific fine-tuning, the robot stably replicated natural human motions in the physical world.

captions.F4: Dynamic validation via contact-implicit iLQR (CI-iLQR). For both the Unitree G1 and Dash robots performing a one-leg hop—a dynamic motion with an extremely narrow support polygon—stable trajectory tracking is achieved while strictly respecting actuator torque limits, as shown in the left leg joint torque trajectories.
captions.F5: Comparison of foot contact between purely kinematic IK (left) and after CI-iLQR refinement (right). While geometric IK causes foot skating on the ground, CI-iLQR resolves MuJoCo dynamics so that ground reaction forces arise properly, producing secure, slip-free foot contact.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: FRDV establishes a scalable foundation for humanoid learning by uniting constrained ultra-fast kinematic retargeting with contact-aware dynamic validation. Despite remaining challenges such as CI-iLQR computational cost and local minima across parallel chunks, the system delivers highly practical results, including real-world robot demonstrations.
sections.details:
FRDV provides a scalable pipeline merging fast SQP with RTI for kinematic retargeting and MuJoCo-based contact-implicit dynamic validation (CI-iLQR). It achieves throughput that dramatically outpaces existing methods (up to 9,156 FPS), demonstrates versatility across 12 humanoid morphologies, ensures high learning performance for downstream RL policies, and successfully deploys zero-shot onto a physical Unitree G1.

At the same time, the paper highlights practical considerations and future challenges:
- **Selectivity in CI-iLQR Usage**: While CI-iLQR resolves contact dynamics to yield high physical fidelity, its computational cost is significantly heavier than kinematic IK. The recommended best practice is not applying it indiscriminately across all data, but rather selectively to motions exhibiting noticeable floating or sliding, or where physical feasibility is questionable.
- **Local Minima in Temporal Chunk Parallelization**: When parallelizing long sequences across time, the non-convex optimization landscape risks neighboring chunks settling into different local minima. While the RefineBoundary step mitigates this, the paper notes that the smoothest results come from solving each individual motion file on a single worker while parallelizing across multiple files.

Future work is expected to further accelerate the dynamic validation stage and enhance solution consistency in parallel optimization.

captions.F6: Snapshot sequence of the zero-shot motion tracking experiment on the physical Unitree G1 humanoid. The RL policy trained on reference trajectories generated by FRDV stably reproduces whole-body human motion without fine-tuning on the real hardware.

takeaways: The key retargeting bottleneck lies in NLP formulation; combining Gauss-Newton approximations for convex QPs with Real-Time Iteration (RTI) unlocks up to 136x speedups (9,156 FPS).
Incorporating self-collision and ground penetration avoidance as capsule-distance inequality constraints directly inside the SQP yields artifact-free motions without post-processing.
Foot skating and floating from kinematic IK can be resolved naturally under MuJoCo physics and torque limits via Contact-Implicit iLQR without explicitly scheduling contact phases.
When parallelizing across massive datasets, parallelizing at the file (clip) level rather than splitting within a single sequence helps avoid discontinuities from non-convex local minima.
limitations: The dynamics validation and refinement stage via Contact-Implicit iLQR is computationally heavy and cannot run at the multi-thousand FPS throughput of the kinematic stage.
Splitting a single motion into temporal chunks for parallelization can lead adjacent chunks to converge to different local minima in the non-convex optimization space, causing discontinuities.
For extreme motions with abrupt transitions such as falling and recovering (FallAndGetUp), sensitivity to early-termination thresholds in downstream RL training can lower policy success rates.
